ariadne in action: common use cases in omics research

Giulio Benedetti

University of Turku
giulio.benedetti@utu.fi

11 November 2026

Source: vignettes/use_cases.Rmd
use_cases.Rmd

ariadne integrates diverse biological resources spanning multiple omics modalities, making it applicable to various omics data science scenarios focused on enriching analyses with curated knowledge from public databases. This tutorial demonstrates the following core applications of ariadne:

Use case Resources Objective
Functional annotation ChocoPhlAn, WoL Annotate microbial or gene features (UniRef) with sequence-based related functional information (e.g., KO, EC, and Pfam)
Taxonomic translation OTT, UniProt Convert taxonomic names and ids across taxonomies (NCBI, SILVA, OTT, etc.)
Set enrichment analysis BugSigDB, GM, GO, MSigDB Test for enriched or depleted functional sets of features between conditions
Pathway enrichment analysis KEGG, Rhea, WoL Test for enriched or depleted metabolic pathways linked to features between conditions
Knowledge-driven association analysis KEGG, UniProt Test previously reported associations between different omics layers (e.g., microbes, metabolites and genes)

First, we load ariadne and additional libraries used across this tutorial.

library(ariadne)
library(anansi)
library(curatedMetagenomicData)
library(mia)
library(miaViz)
library(stringr)
library(DT)

We also import the ariadne resource graph that will be used to link resources throughout this tutorial.

# Import resource graph
graph <- ariadne()

Functional annotation

Resources such as ChocoPhlAn and Web of Life (WoL) have been developed to annotate microbial features and gene families with relevant functional information, including KEGG Orthogroups (KOs), Pfam domains, enzyme commission (EC) numbers and Gene Ontology (GO). This allows to derive actionable insight directly from biological assays.

Resources such as ChocoPhlAn and the Web of Life (WoL) annotate microbial features and gene families with functional metadata—such as KEGG Orthogroups (KOs), Pfam domains, Enzyme Commission (EC) numbers and Gene Ontology (GO) terms—enabling the derivation of biological insights directly from omics datasets.

We import and process the Castro-NallarE_2015 dataset from curatedMetagenomicData, which entails 32 oral cavity microbiome samples from individuals with Chron’s Disease, Type-2 Diabetes and schizophrenia.

We import and preprocess the Castro-NallarE_2015 dataset from curatedMetagenomicData, comprising 32 oral cavity microbiome samples from individuals with Crohn’s disease, Type 2 diabetes and schizophrenia.

# Load gene family experiment
genes <- curatedMetagenomicData(
    "Castro-NallarE_2015.gene_families", dryrun = FALSE
)

# Extract experiment from list
genes <- genes[[1]]

# Keep only unstratified gene families
genes <- genes[str_detect(rownames(genes), fixed("|"), negate = TRUE), ]

# View experiment
genes
#> class: SummarizedExperiment 
#> dim: 651411 32 
#> metadata(0):
#> assays(1): gene_families
#> rownames(651411): UNMAPPED UniRef90_A0A1X3K551 ... UniRef90_A0A091MY75
#>   UniRef90_A0A1I8JMV0
#> rowData names(0):
#> colnames(32): ES_001 ES_007 ... ES_210 ES_211
#> colData names(21): study_name subject_id ... curator antibiotics_family

We query the three shortest paths connecting UniRef90 gene families to Gut Metabolic Modules (GMMs), selecting the primary path mediated by ChocoPhlAn.

# Search first three paths
searchPath(graph, uniref90 ~ gmm, k = 3)
#> Path 1:
#> uniref90 -(ChocoPhlAn)-> ko -(GM)-> gmm
#> 
#> Path 2:
#> uniref90 -(UniProt)-> ec -(KEGG)-> ko -(GM)-> gmm
#> 
#> Path 3:
#> uniref90 -(ChocoPhlAn)-> ec -(KEGG)-> ko -(GM)-> gmm

For users familiar with the bioBakery suite, this operation corresponds to humann_regroup_table from HUMAnN. However, ariadne seamlessly concatenates preliminary and successive mapping steps to directly link distinct feature spaces (e.g., microbes →\rightarrow UniRef →\rightarrow KOs →\rightarrow modules).

# Weave bindings between taxa and GMMs
uniref2gmm <- weaveComplex(graph, uniref90 ~ gmm, init = rownames(genes))
#> uniref90 -(ChocoPhlAn)-> ko
#> ko -(GM)-> gmm

# View linkmap
datatable(uniref2gmm)

Alternatively, WoL can be utilized. Because UniRef-to-KO bindings are exclusive to earlier releases, we explicitly import a previous version of the resource graph.

# Import past release of the resource graph
graph.old <- ariadne(versions = list(WoL = "v20April2021"))

# Weave path through WoL
uniref2gmm <- weaveComplex(
    graph.old,
    uniref90 ~ gmm,
    init = rownames(genes),
    res.name = c("WoL", "GM")
)
#> uniref90 -(WoL)-> ko
#> ko -(GM)-> gmm

Next, we incorporate these mappings into the experiment object and agglomerate the features by set.

# Add sets to experiment side information
genes <- addSets(genes, uniref2gmm, y.names = TRUE)

# Agglomerate experiment by set
set.se <- agglomerateByModule(
    genes, by = "rows", group = levels(uniref2gmm$gmm.name)
)

# View experiment object
set.se
#> class: SummarizedExperiment 
#> dim: 84 32 
#> metadata(0):
#> assays(1): gene_families
#> rownames(84): 4-aminobutyrate degradation acetate to acetyl-CoA ...
#>   valine degradation I xylose degradation
#> rowData names(0):
#> colnames(32): ES_001 ES_007 ... ES_210 ES_211
#> colData names(21): study_name subject_id ... curator antibiotics_family

Finally, per-sample set abundances are visualised using a heatmap.

# Visualise per-sample set abundances
plotHeatmap(set.se, assay.type = "gene_families")

Taxonomic translation

Taxonomic harmonization and cross-referencing across nomenclature systems are frequent bottlenecks in integrative multi-omics analyses. ariadne facilitates robust ID translation and name resolution across diverse taxonomies (e.g., NCBI, SILVA, OTT and Greengenes).

First, we load the built-in butyrate linkmap containing microbial features associated with butyrate biosynthesis.

# Import butyrate linkmap
data("butyrate", package = "ariadne")

# View butyrate linkmap
datatable(butyrate)

We map NCBI taxon identifiers to their corresponding binomial names.

# Link taxon ids to names
tax2name <- linkNames(graph, "taxid", ids = butyrate$taxid)

# View linkmap
datatable(tax2name)

Conversely, NCBI taxon IDs can be retrieved from taxon names, which need to be exact.

# Link taxon names to ids
name2tax <- linkNames(graph, "taxid", names = butyrate$taxid.name)
#> Warning: ids for 1 taxid names not found.

# View linkmap
datatable(name2tax)

Alternatively, we can query the Open Tree of Life Taxonomy (OTT) to resolve taxon names using approximate string matching, accommodating partial or imprecise entries.

# Link taxon names to OTT ids
name2ott <- linkNames(graph, "ott", names = butyrate$taxid.name)

# Map OTT ids to NCBI taxon ids
name2tax <- weavePath(graph, ott.name ~ taxid, init = rev(name2ott))
#> ott stratified by ott.name
#> ott -(OTT)-> taxid

# View linkmap
datatable(name2tax)

OTT also bridges disparate taxonomies. Here, we translate NCBI taxon IDs from the butyrate linkmap to corresponding SILVA SSU identifiers.

# Convert taxid to silva
tax2silva <- weavePath(
    graph,
    taxid ~ silva_ssu,
    init = butyrate$taxid,
    use.names = FALSE
)
#> taxid -(OTT)-> silva_ssu

# View linkmap
datatable(tax2silva)

Similarly, WoL enables the translation of Greengenes identifiers to NCBI taxon IDs.

# Convert greengenes to taxid
gg2tax <- weavePath(graph, greengenes ~ taxid)
#> greengenes -(WoL)-> wol
#> wol -(WoL)-> taxid
#> Warning: names for 2 taxid ids not found.

# View linkmap
datatable(gg2tax)

Set enrichment analysis

Leveraging prior functional or phenotypic annotations, set enrichment analysis tests whether predefined feature sets (genes, taxa, or metabolites) are over- or under-represented. Common repositories include GO or MSigDB for genes and BugSigDB for microbial signatures.

Feature sets of interest can be queried via keyword matching against descriptive names. For instance, we extract attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)-related microbial signatures from BugSigDB via the ariadne graph.

# Retrieve all unique BugSig sets
bugsig2name <- linkNames(graph, "bugsig")

# Extract sets related to ADHD
adhd.sets <- bugsig2name[str_detect(bugsig2name$bugsig.name, fixed("ADHD")), ]

# View sets of interest
datatable(adhd.sets)

We load and preprocess the Tengeler2020 dataset, comprising stool metagenomic and metabolomic profiles from humanised ADHD mice.

# Import experiment object
data("Tengeler2020", package = "mia")

# Rename experiment object
tse <- Tengeler2020

# Transform counts to relative abundance
tse <- transformAssay(tse, method = "relabundance")

# View experiment object
tse
#> class: TreeSummarizedExperiment 
#> dim: 151 27 
#> metadata(0):
#> assays(2): counts relabundance
#> rownames(151): Bacteroides Bacteroides_1 ... Parabacteroides_8
#>   Unidentified_Lachnospiraceae_14
#> rowData names(6): Kingdom Phylum ... Family Genus
#> colnames(27): A110 A12 ... A35 A38
#> colData names(4): patient_status cohort patient_status_vs_cohort
#>   sample_name
#> reducedDimNames(0):
#> mainExpName: NULL
#> altExpNames(0):
#> rowLinks: a LinkDataFrame (151 rows)
#> rowTree: 1 phylo tree(s) (151 leaves)
#> colLinks: NULL
#> colTree: NULL

We map microbial features at the genus level to their corresponding OTT taxon IDs to establish initial values for graph traversal.

# Link taxon names to OTT ids
name2tax <- linkNames(graph, "ott", names = rowData(tse)$Genus)
#> Warning: ids for 40 ott names not found.

# View linkmap
datatable(name2tax)

We weave a path from OTT taxon names to BugSig sets via OTT IDs, yielding a linkmap directly compatible with our experiment object.

# Weave path from OTT taxon names to bugsig
tax2bugsig <- weavePath(graph, ott.name ~ bugsig, init = rev(name2tax))
#> ott stratified by ott.name
#> ott -(OTT)-> taxid
#> taxid -(BugSigDB)-> bugsig

# View linkmap
datatable(tax2bugsig)

This can be added to the experiment object and used to agglomerate the assay by set, which returns the per-sample abundance for each set.

# Add set information to experiment
tse <- addSets(tse, tax2bugsig, key = "Genus", y.names = TRUE)

# Limit sets to those found by weave (add support to agglomerateByModule)
adhd.sets <- adhd.sets[adhd.sets$bugsig %in% levels(tax2bugsig$bugsig), ]

# Agglomerate experiment by set
adhd.se <- agglomerateByModule(tse, by = "rows", group = adhd.sets$bugsig.name)

# View results
adhd.se
#> class: TreeSummarizedExperiment 
#> dim: 7 27 
#> metadata(0):
#> assays(2): counts relabundance
#> rownames(7): ADHD_vs_Controls_UP ADHD_vs_Controls_DOWN ...
#>   Medicated-ADHD-(ADHD-+-MPH)_vs_Unmedicated-ADHD_UP
#>   Medicated-ADHD-(ADHD-+-MPH)_vs_Unmedicated-ADHD_DOWN
#> rowData names(0):
#> colnames(27): A110 A12 ... A35 A38
#> colData names(4): patient_status cohort patient_status_vs_cohort
#>   sample_name
#> reducedDimNames(0):
#> mainExpName: NULL
#> altExpNames(0):
#> rowLinks: NULL
#> rowTree: NULL
#> colLinks: NULL
#> colTree: NULL

Finally, we visualise per-sample set abundances using a heatmap.

# Visualise per-sample set abundance
plotHeatmap(adhd.se, assay.type = "relabundance", col.var = "patient_status")

Pathway enrichment analysis

Analogous to set enrichment, pathway enrichment analysis tests for enriched or depleted metabolic pathways based on feature coverage. Representative resources include KEGG and MetaCyc for comprehensive microbial metabolism, alongside specialised databases like enviPath for xenobiotic biotransformation.

KEGG pathways can be mapped from KOs or ECs, ideally via KEGG reactions.

# Search paths from ec to kegg pathways
searchPath(graph, ec ~ kegg_path, include = "kegg_rxn", k = 3)
#> Path 1:
#> ec -(KEGG)-> kegg_rxn -(KEGG)-> kegg_path
#> 
#> Path 2:
#> ec -(KEGG)-> kegg_rxn -(KEGG)-> rclass -(KEGG)-> kegg_path
#> 
#> Path 3:
#> ec -(KEGG)-> kegg_glycan -(KEGG)-> kegg_rxn -(KEGG)-> kegg_path

We link EC numbers to KEGG pathways while specifying a custom coverage threshold.

# Weave path from ec to kegg pathways
ec2path <- weaveComplex(
    graph,
    ec ~ kegg_path,
    include = "kegg_rxn",
    threshold = 0.5
)
#> ec -(KEGG)-> kegg_rxn
#> kegg_rxn -(KEGG)-> kegg_path

# View linkmap
datatable(ec2path)

The MetaCyc pathways are provided by WoL2. However, they correspond to an earlier version of MetaCyc before it became commercially available.

# Search paths from ec to metacyc pathways
searchPath(graph, ec ~ metacyc_path, k = 3)
#> Path 1:
#> ec -(WoL)-> metacyc_rxn -(WoL)-> metacyc_path
#> 
#> Path 2:
#> ec -(Rhea)-> rhea -(Rhea)-> metacyc_rxn -(WoL)-> metacyc_path
#> 
#> Path 3:
#> ec -(GO)-> go -(GO)-> metacyc_rxn -(WoL)-> metacyc_path

Similarly, EC numbers are linked to associated MetaCyc pathways while also estimating pathway coverage by feature.

# Weave path from ec to metacyc pathways
ec2path <- weaveComplex(graph, ec ~ metacyc_path)
#> ec -(WoL)-> metacyc_rxn
#> metacyc_rxn -(WoL)-> metacyc_path
#> Warning: names for 1287 ec ids not found.

# View linkmap
datatable(ec2path)
#> Warning in instance$preRenderHook(instance): It seems your data is too big for
#> client-side DataTables. You may consider server-side processing:
#> https://rstudio.github.io/DT/server.html

Knowledge-driven association analysis

anansi evaluates pairwise associations between dual-omics modalities (e.g., microbiome and metabolome) within a unified experiment, restricting statistical comparisons to prior biologically relevant or documented interactions. ariadne supplies the necessary relational mappings to constrain this search space.

We load the HintikkaXOData dataset, including stool metabolomic and metagenomic profiles from mice subjected to low and high-fat dietary regimes.

# Import dataset
data("HintikkaXOData", package = "mia")

# Rename object
mae <- HintikkaXOData

# View multi-assay experiment
mae
#> A MultiAssayExperiment object of 3 listed
#>  experiments with user-defined names and respective classes.
#>  Containing an ExperimentList class object of length 3:
#>  [1] microbiota: TreeSummarizedExperiment with 12706 rows and 40 columns
#>  [2] metabolites: TreeSummarizedExperiment with 38 rows and 40 columns
#>  [3] biomarkers: TreeSummarizedExperiment with 39 rows and 40 columns
#> Functionality:
#>  experiments() - obtain the ExperimentList instance
#>  colData() - the primary/phenotype DataFrame
#>  sampleMap() - the sample coordination DataFrame
#>  `$`, `[`, `[[` - extract colData columns, subset, or experiment
#>  *Format() - convert into a long or wide DataFrame
#>  assays() - convert ExperimentList to a SimpleList of matrices
#>  exportClass() - save data to flat files

We agglomerate the microbiome experiment by Genus and sanitise feature names to maximise their successful conversion to OTT taxon ids.

# Agglomerate microbiome experiment by Genus
mae[["microbiota"]] <- agglomerateByRank(mae[["microbiota"]], rank = "Genus")
#> Duplicated labels were made unique.

# Remove rank prefix from taxon names
rownames(mae[["microbiota"]]) <- mae[["microbiota"]] |>
    rownames() |>
    str_remove(fixed("D_5__"))

# Link taxon names to OTT ids
name2tax <- linkNames(graph, "ott", names = rownames(mae[["microbiota"]]))
#> Warning: ids for 70 ott names not found.

# View linkmap
datatable(name2tax)

We map metabolite identifiers to corresponding KEGG compound IDs. In practice, unmatched entries typically require manual curation.

# Link metabolite names to KEGG compound ids
name2cpd <- linkNames(
    graph,
    "kegg_cpd",
    names = rownames(mae[["metabolites"]])
)
#> Warning: ids for 9 kegg_cpd names not found.

# View linkmap
datatable(name2cpd)

We then weave the path linking taxon names to KEGG compound IDs.

# Weave path from taxon names to KEGG compound ids
tax2cpd <- weavePath(
    graph,
    ott.name ~ kegg_cpd,
    init = rev(name2tax),
    res.name = c("OTT", "WoL", "KEGG")
)
#> ott stratified by ott.name
#> ott -(OTT)-> taxid
#> taxid -(WoL)-> wol
#> wol -(WoL)-> metacyc_prt
#> metacyc_prt -(WoL)-> metacyc_enzrxn
#> metacyc_enzrxn -(WoL)-> metacyc_rxn
#> metacyc_rxn -(WoL)-> ec
#> ec -(KEGG)-> kegg_cpd

# Remove KEGG compound id column
tax2cpd$kegg_cpd <- NULL

# Rename linkmap variables
names(tax2cpd) <- c("microbiota", "metabolites")

# Fix this behaviour in anansi
tax2cpd <- tax2cpd[tax2cpd$microbiota %in% rownames(mae[["microbiota"]]), ]
tax2cpd <- tax2cpd[tax2cpd$metabolites %in% rownames(mae[["metabolites"]]), ]
tax2cpd[] <- lapply(tax2cpd, factor)

# View linkmap
datatable(tax2cpd)

Finally, we construct an anansi Web object and execute the association analysis.

# Create anansi web object
web <- weaveWeb(
    mae,
    tableX = "microbiota",
    tableY = "metabolites",
    link = tax2cpd
)
#> Dropped features in tableX: 8 remain.
#> Dropped features in tableY: 18 remain.

# Perform association analysis
out <- anansi(
    web = web,
    formula = ~ Diet,
    adjust.method = "BH"
)
#> Fitting least-squares for following model:
#> ~ x + Diet + x:Diet
#> Warning in cor(x = web@tableY[group.bool, ], y = web@tableX[group.bool, : the
#> standard deviation is zero
#> Running correlations for the following groups:
#>  High-fat, High-fat + XOS, Low-fat, Low-fat + XOS
#> Warning in cor(x = web@tableY[group.bool, ], y = web@tableX[group.bool, : the
#> standard deviation is zero
#> Warning in cor(x = web@tableY[group.bool, ], y = web@tableX[group.bool, : the
#> standard deviation is zero
#> Warning in cor(x = web@tableY[group.bool, ], y = web@tableX[group.bool, : the
#> standard deviation is zero
#> Warning in cor(x = web@tableY[group.bool, ], y = web@tableX[group.bool, : the
#> standard deviation is zero

# Sort results by p-value
out <- out[order(out$full_p.values), ]

# View results
datatable(out)

Resulting associations are visualised via a forest plot.

# Fix this behaviour in anansi
# Visualise associations
# plotAnansi(
#     out,
#     association.type = "disjointed",
#     model.var = "Diet"
# )
